vignette:
He is 63 now, a commercial airline pilot with decades of experience, the kind of man who still irons his shirts with care and checks the weather twice before leaving for the airport. Colleagues know him as steady, precise, and difficult to rattle. His wife knows the cost of that steadiness. She has lived beside the tension in him for years, felt it in the way his shoulders harden at sudden sounds, in the way he scans every room before he sits down, in the way sleep turns him into someone she cannot reach.

He grew up in Oceania and joined the military as a young man, before aviation became his civilian life. At first he talks about that period the way many veterans do, with flat facts and no adjectives. He says where he was deployed, what his unit was asked to do, the heat, the noise, the waiting. Only after several sessions does the story become personal. He describes one operation in particular, a combat engagement that began with confusion and ended in blood, fire, and the deaths of men he knew well. He remembers the smell first, then the sound of screaming over radio traffic, then the surreal clarity of noticing small things that should not have mattered in that moment. He had to keep moving, keep following orders, even while stepping around bodies and trying not to look too long at the face of a friend who had been alive an hour earlier.

What stays with him is not only terror but the sense that something in him closed that day. He returns home carrying images he cannot place anywhere. In the beginning he tells himself this is normal, that discipline will handle it. He avoids talking about what happened, even with other veterans. When memories force their way in, he pushes them down by keeping busy. He learns to function at a high level. He marries, builds a life, and enters civilian aviation, where control, procedure, and composure are rewarded. In the cockpit he feels most like himself. There are checklists, instruments, rules for emergencies. There is a right action for nearly everything.

But outside that structured world, the war leaks through. Sleep becomes the first casualty. He dreads going to bed because dreams bring him back to the engagement with a vividness that leaves him disoriented and drenched in sweat. His wife wakes to him shouting, sometimes striking out before he fully knows where he is. More than once he has fallen asleep on the sofa because he does not want to risk another night of waking beside her in that state. He tells her he is just a light sleeper, just stressed, but both of them know that is not the whole truth.

During the day he lives in a state of guarded alertness. He sits where he can see exits. In restaurants he tracks who comes through the door and who is carrying what. Fireworks, helicopters, even a car backfiring can send a jolt through him so strong that his heart races and his hands shake. When that happens, he is no longer fully in the present. For a moment he is back there, his body reacting before thought catches up. He is ashamed of these moments, especially when they happen in public, and he covers them with irritation. His family experiences him as impatient, easily angered, and emotionally far away. He can discuss aircraft systems for an hour, but if his wife asks what he is feeling, he goes quiet or leaves the room.

The work that once gave him refuge has become more complicated with age. He is still meticulous, but he notices how exhausting it is to stay so tightly controlled. Before flights he sleeps poorly in hotels, waking at every hallway noise. He checks locks repeatedly. On layovers he avoids crowded hotel bars and declines social invitations from crew, preferring the safety of solitude even though he feels lonely in it. He keeps his suitcase packed with military neatness and feels unreasonably tense when anything is out of place.

He rarely allows himself to think about the men who died, but guilt lives close to the surface. He wonders why he survived when others did not, and whether there was something more he should have done. Anniversaries of the combat incident darken his mood in ways he cannot explain to others. He becomes withdrawn, drinks more than usual, and finds himself staring into space, caught by images he has spent years trying not to see. His wife says he is present in the house but absent from their life.

What troubles him most now is how little time seems to have passed inside his body. Intellectually he knows he is a 63-year-old pilot, husband, and grandfather. Yet when he wakes from a nightmare or startles at a sound, he is again the young serviceman in combat, braced for death. He says he has spent most of his adult life flying above the earth, calm at thirty thousand feet, while part of him remains fixed on the ground in that one terrible place, still waiting for the next explosion.
